book: 033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_
essays: “I Dare You to Watch This Show!”
This Has All Happened Before and It Will All Happen Again
Who They Are or Who They Want to Be
It’s the Disappointing Stories that Sound True to Life
samples: Show writer David Weddle recounts how Ron Moore pushed him and Brad Thompson to abandon Star Trek-style expository dialogue and tell 'Act of Contrition' through flashbacks interleaved with the present, dramatizing Starbuck's guilt over passing Zak Adama on his flight test. He argues this unlocked a stream-of-consciousness mode — dreams, hallucinations, and memories flowing out of characters' inner emotional lives — that the series extended in episodes like 'Scar,' 'Maelstrom,' and 'Unfinished Business,' echoing Faulkner's 'the past isn't even past.' The foreword is a creator's testimony that BSG's scrambled-chronology storytelling is what made the show worthy of a book of philosophical readings.

Editor Josef Steiff's introduction traces Galactica from Glen Larson's 1978 series and Galactica 1980 through the Moore/Eick re-imagining, and frames the show through Edward James Olmos's campus talks, where he 'dares' audiences to watch a series he calls truth about identity, race, culture, and purpose. It endorses Orson Scott Card's claim that true science fiction, like religious literature, asks who we are, what our place in the universe is, and how we find or make meaning. It closes by explaining the book's Cylon naming conventions (Sixes, Eights, Boomers, Athenas) and its gimmick of five unattributed 'Final Five' chapters.

Milsky uses Ricoeur and MacIntyre's narrative theory of personal identity to read the two Sharons: Boomer's fabricated human backstory suffers a 'factual disruption' when she shoots Adama, while Athena's 'disruption of belief' comes from falling in love with Helo. He argues such disruptions — also suffered by humans like Starbuck (recovered memories of abuse in 'Maelstrom'), Roslin (coming to believe she is Pythia's dying leader), and Helo — need not destroy identity, since narratives can be retold, as the Final Four do in 'Crossroads, Part 2' with Tigh's 'My name is Saul Tigh' speech. Third-party narratives (Six disowning Athena, the crew refusing to see Boomer as Boomer) show identity is partly socially constructed and can become self-fulfilling prophecy, with Boomer's blackouts resembling dissociative identity disorder.

Booth argues that the 'Resistance' webisodes fracture BSG's narrative across television and Internet, forcing viewers to actively construct the story — Jammer's execution in 'Collaborators' and Duck's suicide bombing only make full sense if you pieced the webisodes together — and that this viewer-side fragmentation mirrors the characters' fractured identities. Drawing on Foucault's constructed self, Deleuze and Guattari's 'schizophrenia,' Goffman's performed roles, and Haraway's cyborg, he reads Baltar's 'Am I a Cylon?', Boomer's amnesia in 'Water,' Hera's human-Cylon hybridity, and Tigh's choice in 'Crossroads' to actively construct who he will be. The payoff: there is no central location for the self, the narrative, or Cylonhood — each becomes whole only through active construction.

Cuddy asks how gamers relate to BSG videogame avatars — as an extension of the ego or a disposable other — using Freud's id/ego/superego to cast the avatar as a socially safe venue for reconciling forbidden desires (piloting a Cylon Raider) with the superego's demands. Against Rehak's claim that gamers simply drop the avatar when losing, he enlists Sartre: blaming the game or 'cheating' opponents is bad faith, a denial of the freedom to create one's own essence, with Lee's '33' debate about responsibility for the Olympic Carrier and Baltar's vacillation as in-show parallels. Sartre's facticity bounds the freedom — hard missions are fixed facts to deal with — so the gamer, like Adama's fleet, must take responsibility within limits.

The chapter reads Baltar's Head-Six (and Caprica Six's Head-Baltar) through the gothic Double and Doppelgänger tradition, re-imagined via dissociative identity disorder: Baltar splits off his guilt over the genocide into a female doppelgänger who lets him evade responsibility, as in 'Precipice' where he finds the execution order signed without any memory of signing it. It then links this doubling to Plato's Symposium myth of lovers as split halves seeking their other half, since Baltar cannot function without some version of Six. Its resolution is Aristotle's golden mean: virtue is not choosing one self over another but balancing extremes, for individuals and for humanity and its Double, the Cylons — with Hera as the embodied balance.

book: 034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch
essays: What Do We Hear when We Listen to Our iPods
Progress Is a Myth that Truly Makes Life Worthwhile
Modding Mavens and the Limits of Reification
samples: Wittkower opens with his cat Wallace at the window to show hearing is selective, then applies Sartre's account of the Look -- the voyeur at the keyhole hearing a footstep, the other as a 'void within being' -- to ask when sounds announce another person, the iPod-era rustle becoming the sudden 'appearance of a face.' Drawing on Marx's early claim that our senses are socially estranged, so that we meet others only as waiters, clerks, and price tags ('we are not our khakis'), he argues the audio cocoon both limits and enables encounter: mostly we hear our own identity reflected back ('I am the kind of person who listens to Amy Winehouse'). The governing image is Odysseus lashed to the mast, hearing the Sirens without being able to act, and the chapter closes by rehabilitating Marx as the first philosopher of technology alongside Heidegger, Dewey, Lukacs, Adorno, and Habermas.

Rehn argues there is no essential definition of the iPod: Shuffle, Nano, Classic, and Touch share only overlapping, criss-crossing similarities, exactly as Wittgenstein's family resemblance handles 'sport' (water polo vs. boxing) and 'game.' Even Cover Flow -- a physically impossible floating cascade of albums -- feels instantly familiar, showing familiarity is something users construct from hints rather than perceive, and syncing, playlists, and the Music Quiz game endlessly re-manufacture it (the iPod as the new McDonald's golden arches abroad). Flipping the relation via Actor-Network Theory, he notes the iPod tracks play counts, pushes 'Listeners Also Bought,' and trains our flicking gestures, so that perhaps the iPod becomes familiar with us; the Microsoft Zune figures as the abject, zombie-like copy whose perverse familiarity reveals a politics of recognition, and the closing game of imagining Wittgenstein's playlist endorses natural language's many language games over exact definitions.

Raven reads design history as a pendulum between 'Beauty Waves' (Art Nouveau's sinuous decoration, 1960s psychedelia) and 'Truth Waves' (Art Deco functionalism, Le Corbusier's 'machine for living'), poles he grounds in Berkeley's 'esse est percipi' idealism versus metaphysical realism. The late-1990s blobject -- the iMac, the New Beetle, the MACH3 razor -- begins merging the waves through computer-aided design, and the iPod, launched five weeks after 9/11 and named for Kubrick's pod ('Open the pod bay door, Hal'), is the 'minimalist blobject' or 'squircle' where the merger completes. Reading the moment through Heidegger's claim that technology transforms human existence 'in its innermost recesses' and through Freud's pleasure versus reality principles, he argues the Iraq War sealed the reality principle into consumer design: 'our iPods now have edges.'

Garnar contrasts the material practice of collecting CDs -- shelving some 1,500-2,000 discs by genre, the Rachels' Egon Schiele packaging, and Humean associations binding particular discs to memories like buying blue hair dye the day he got New Order's Lowlife -- with the iPod-era 'iPhenomenon' of buying songs piecemeal from iTunes. Using William James's question 'How is the practice real?' he rejects the real/virtual split, and reads the freedom of iMedia as a corollary of Marx and Engels's 'single, unconscionable freedom -- Free Trade': the solipsistic consumer never confronts the artist the way the album as artifact (Coltrane's My Favorite Things ending, he realizes, had to end with 'But Not for Me') forces him to. The body supposedly made unnecessary by 'iLiving' remains, with Foucault, a site of discipline -- eating disorders, outsourced assembly labor, e-waste -- so he keeps his iPod but defends a plurality of media and calls progress a myth.

Schaeffer starts from the felt aliveness of the click wheel -- 'it whirs and clicks, demanding my attention' -- and argues we personify iPods precisely because mass production hides their makers, applying Marx's account of alienation and reification ('the personification of things and the reification of persons') to the Foxconn 'iPod City' exposé of fifteen-hour shifts and hundred-worker dorm rooms paid fifty dollars a month. Extending the analysis through Lukacs, he reads Apple's fluctuating stock price as 'phantom objectivity' and the iPod bubbles of his Brooklyn coffee shop and his classroom -- couples passing 'like ships in the night' -- as a reified world that appears as the only possible world. Against the thesis's bleakness, modders -- a bicycle-dynamo charger, a fist-sized remote with five large switches built for visually impaired users -- re-inscribe humanity into the commodity, marking the limits of reification.

This chapter is a transcript of LibriVox Community Podcast show #20, in which host Jim Mowatt and guests discuss recording philosophy texts as free audiobooks, sparked by volunteers' 'enthusiasm' over a group recording of Kant's Critique of Pure Reason and a fierce forum debate over which translation to use. Editor D.E. Wittkower and his dyslexic student testify that audio opens dense texts to readers who otherwise reread thirty or forty pages to a headache, while volunteer M.L. Cohen argues that recording forces slow, attentive reading and that -- as with orphan drugs -- market logic explains why commercial audiobooks ignore the philosophical canon; audio supplements but never replaces careful reading.

book: 035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant
essays: Ex Astris, Scientia GEORGE A REISCH
“All Good Things Must Come to an End”
“Condemned to Be a Member of This Lowest of Species”
“Sometimes You Just Have to Bow to the Absurd”
“Obviously, the Borg Can’t Hold Their Liquor”
Emergentism Now Can Scotty Beam Us Up
“Logic Is the Beginning of Wisdom . . . Not the End”
samples: The editors' introduction takes Starfleet Academy's motto 'Ex Astris, Scientia' as its frame: Picard handing cadet Wesley Crusher a book by William James shows officers need philosophy, not just ship operations, and the starry-heavens motif runs from Thales and Plato's cave through Kant's 'moral law within and starry heavens above.' It surveys the book's Trek dilemmas (Picard and Dathon's alien language, Data's emotion chip, Khan's vengeance, Riker's Q powers) as 2,500-year-old philosophical problems, and argues Trek's optimism — Picard's 'the acquisition of wealth is no longer the driving force' — restates Aristotle's claim that all humans by nature desire to know. Like philosophy from Socrates on, Trek is presented as 'an entertaining, edifying preparation' for living by one's ideals, a life-education primer sealed with Roddenberry's advice to 'slip in a heavy idea or two.'

Cantor argues the TNG episode 'Darmok' dramatizes Wittgenstein's later philosophy of language: Picard first reads Dathon's 'Temba, his arms wide' as naming objects — the Augustinian picture of language Wittgenstein rejects — then realizes on El-Adrel IV that Tamarian utterances mean through their use in a shared activity, as when he and Dathon fight the beast together. The Tamarians speak entirely in citations of their own myths ('Darmok and Jalad at Tanagra', 'Shaka, when the walls fell'), so language is shown to be embedded in a form of life, exactly Wittgenstein's 'if a lion could talk' problem. The chapter then ties this to E.D. Hirsch's cultural literacy — Troi's 'Juliet on her balcony' and Picard's Gilgamesh story show communication presupposes shared cultural knowledge — and concludes that the erudite writers Menosky and LaZebnik made a genuinely philosophic episode of television.

Writing as a Vulcan philosophy professor and student of Spock, the chapter reconstructs Vulcan civilization from Surak's Awakening as three interlocking modes of logic — formal logic (whose first law, Kiri-kin-tha's 'nothing unreal exists', parallels Parmenides), ethical logic (the axiom 'the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few'), and meditative discipline — and maps them onto Patanjali's Yoga: the yamas, meditation, and samadhi's cosmic oneness, with ahimsa linking Surak to Gandhi and King. It then rereads Star Trek: The Motion Picture, where V'Ger's pure logic leaves both it and Spock asking 'Is this all that I am?', and Spock's mind meld with V'Ger becomes a tantric union that integrates feeling with logic after the failure of Kolinahr. The chapter's thesis is that 'logic without need is sterile': logic is 'the beginning of wisdom . . . not the end', and Spock's rebirth culminates in choosing the human thing precisely when it is not the logical thing.

Thorsrud casts Spock and Data's exchange in 'Unification, Part II' — Spock dispassionate by choice, Data longing for emotion — as a replay of the ancient debate between Stoics and Peripatetics over whether to eliminate or moderate the passions. The Aristotelian side is built from Data's emotion-chip rage while killing a Borg ('Descent'), his unfelt breakup with Jenna ('In Theory'), and Riker's defense of trust after Ishara's betrayal ('Legacy'): emotions are judgments with pleasure or pain, there is a right amount to feel, and invulnerability costs the 'emotional bonds that make us who we are.' The Stoic reply uses Epictetus's distinction between involuntary impressions and assent (Picard's fear on the Borg ship vs. the holodeck), Cicero's refusal to 'moderate' what is simply a fault, and Seneca on anger, exemplified by Spock's 'quite logical relief' in 'Amok Time', his calculated desperation in 'The Galileo Seven', and his saving the bigot Stiles in 'Balance of Terror' — leaving the Peripatetic conclusion that fortune's goods are not mere indifferents and we may rightly 'smile with so little provocation.'

Biderman and Devlin read The Wrath of Khan as a Nietzschean test of whether revenge can ground a meaningful life after the death of God: Kirk, stuck 'flying a goddamn computer console' as an admiral, and the Genesis project seek meaning through creation without God, while Khan, broken by exile on Ceti Alpha V, chooses vengeance. Using Nozick's contrast between impartial retribution and personally satisfying revenge, and Nietzsche's will to power, master-slave morality, and ressentiment, they argue Khan had the superhuman gifts and independence from herd morality of a candidate Overman, but let revenge enslave him — culminating in Genesis turned weapon and his dying 'For hate's sake . . . I spit my last breath at thee,' a resounding No to life. Spock's mirror-image self-sacrifice, which affirms life, is offered as the better Nietzschean Overman.

Arp uses Glaucon's Ring of Gyges from the Republic to ask whether unlimited power must corrupt the just: Q's career of meddling ('Encounter at Farpoint', 'Q Who?', 'The Q and the Grey') shows the corrupted case, while Riker given Q-powers in 'Hide and Q' helps his friends instead, a counterexample Glaucon can resist by pleading insufficient time. He then explains the Q's misery — Quinn's bored suicidal plea in 'Death Wish' — through the hedonistic paradox, refining it with Mill's distinction between bodily lower pleasures and mental higher ones and Aristotle's account of the lasting pleasure of completed states like beating the ship's computer at chess. The conclusion is that Q's 'condemnation' to mortality in 'Déjà Q' reveals the human condition as enviable: it is precisely our lacking unlimited power, pleasure, and immortality that drives the striving for truth, justice, goodness, and love.

book: 036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am
essays: Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight
Can We Play Beyond Good and Evil
Solutions to the Problem The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the
The Triforce Holds a Prosperous Future
The Lesson and Legacy of Din, Nayru, and Farore
samples: Editor Luke Cuddy's introduction: he argues videogames, and the Zelda franchise in particular, deserve philosophical attention, then frames the book's spirit with Plato's Meno. Just as Socrates' questioning leads the slave boy from thinking he knows to actually knowing that a double-sized square has area sixteen, the gamer's struggle through dungeons is rewarded with the item-room fanfare (the ladder, the silver arrow) as an 'AHA!' feeling of insight. The chapter lists the franchise's games and the book's guiding questions, stressing that the gamer guides Link rather than passively watching.

Frome tackles the paradox of fiction through Wind Waker: why do we fear Gohma, feel sad when Link leaves his grandmother on Outset Island, or care when Tetra's identity is revealed, though we know none of it is real? He rejects the illusion theory (we never suspend disbelief enough to call the police), Carroll's thought theory (fear is too fast and too vivid for mere thoughts), and Walton's pretend theory (involuntary pretending and the uniform way all players see the sail break it). Instead he argues for a multi-level mind, modeled on Plato's divided soul in the Republic and Fodor's mental modules: local unconscious appraisals react to the fire as if real, while a global appraisal of reality-status keeps us in our chairs.

Wilson argues that Wind Waker's Ballad of Gales warp sacrifices environmental presence for goal-oriented play: the long, uneventful sails where waves, cloud patterns, and quiet soundscapes dominate are precisely when Hyrule feels like a place, and teleporting turns it into a disposable grid of destinations. Drawing on Castells' spaces of flows versus places, Schivelbusch's 'annihilation of space and time' by the railway (the player becomes a 'human parcel'), and de Certeau's opposition between the panoptic map view and the embodied everyday view, he contends the very existence of the warp option colors all distance traveled. Even panoramic pleasures like hang-gliding over Outset Island, he notes, must be balanced against pure map-grid travel.

Arp and Milarker use Zelda examples to teach informal logic: Rob's 'all gamers are geeks' is a hasty generalization, the argument that the original Zelda is chronologically first commits equivocation (Earth release order is not Hyrule chronology, since Miyamoto named Ocarina of Time earliest), and debates over banning violent games trade in false dilemmas, ad hominem, and slippery slopes. The chapter sets out premises, conclusions, deductive versus inductive arguments, validity and soundness, strength and cogency, with worked examples from Clawshot reasoning to Best Buy Wii lines. Its point is that fallacious reasoning harms real lives, so readers should audit every argument in the book and in the gaming world.

Fellela reads Link's endless drudgery (slashing grass for rupees, collecting bottles, leaving the final Ganon fight at a 'permanent pause') through existentialism: Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' is dramatized in Ocarina of Time's opening, where Link must acquire sword, fairy, and skills to make himself the hero, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead' call to become gods is answered by Link restoring meaning to a hostile Hyrule. Camus' Sisyphus figures the repetitive world-saving quest as an absurd hero's owned task, and Frankl's logotherapy (meaning as the tension between what one is and what one should become) explains why humiliating menial tasks, in camp or in laundromats or in Zelda, become bearable and even meaningful. Link's fixed options even illustrate Frankl's point that freedom is the stance we take toward conditions, not freedom from them.

Janssen argues Zelda is quietly obsessed with death: turning the console off models death as pure absence of experience, which we cannot otherwise comprehend, and gives the gamer a comforting structured formula in place of a chaotic universe. Link, resurrected endlessly to serve the player, is condemned to Hegelian purgatory and what Bernard Williams called the tedium of immortality, while dungeon bosses, who die once and stay dead, are the only genuinely mortal, hence most human, beings in Hyrule. The Wind Waker prologue's eternally returning Hero does suggest Plato-style dualism with an immortal soul, but the chapter notes that Nietzsche's assault on faith destroyed dualism's credibility, leaving the series as a vessel for both materialist nothingness and romantic reincarnation.

book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West
essays: Dorothy Growing Up in the Land of Oz
Dorothy and the Art of War
“Here, Here, What’s All This Jabber-wapping When There’s Work to Be Done ”
Conscious Unity “There’s No Place Like Home”
Wait, Did I Hit Pause Where’d the Remote Get to . .
As Nasty as I Wanna Be
samples: The editors' introduction argues that Oz endures because it is not one story but a shifting plurality of tales (storyteller Chris Chandler's point, likening it to the Iliad), which each reader can enter through any character, from the Lion to, after Gregory Maguire, the Wicked Witch herself. It models the volume's method with a small logical puzzle about 'there's no place like home'—the phrase is negative because Dorothy herself is part of what home means, so Kansas has a new Dorothy—and previews the book's recurring questions: the Yellow Brick Road as a many-meaninged journey metaphor, the virtues of brain, heart, and courage, evil (why must a little girl kill the Witch?), and the reality-status of Oz versus Kansas.

Luke Dick stages Immanuel Kant as the 'Supreme Critical Chancellor of Munchkinland' and runs the film through Kantian ethics: against hedonism, utilitarianism, and command-based religion, the formula of universalizability condemns the Wizard's lies and his use of the companions as mere means, while the ends-in-themselves principle raises the awkward case of Glinda and Dorothy keeping the dead Witch of the East's ruby slippers. Judging the characters, the Lion's rescue of Dorothy is morally praiseworthy (duty against strong inclination), the brainless Scarecrow falls outside Kant's jurisdiction, and the sentimental Tin Man is pre-emptively condemned. The chapter finally rebels against its Chancellor: cases like returning the slippers, or Toto versus Almira Gulch, show that a world of absolute morality lies only 'somewhere over the rainbow,' and real moral life in Kansas needs Baum's Tin Man heart reconciled with Kantian duty.

McCall and Auxier use Aristotle's virtue ethics to unpack the Wizard's claim to be 'a good man but a bad wizard' and to argue that no external token—the diploma, heart watch, or medal—can confer virtue, which is cultivated only through practice and experience. Each companion lacks something specific: the Scarecrow the intellectual virtues and phronesis, the Tin Man the feelings and stable states of character that regulate emotion, the Lion the sophrosyne that balances thinking and feeling into courage as the mean between recklessness and cowardice. Aristotle's three grades of friendship (utility, pleasure, virtue) frame the companions' bond with Dorothy, and MacIntyre's account of virtues internal to practices explains why the Wizard's public recognition still matters. Dorothy herself begins as the child Aristotle says cannot yet be virtuous—fleeing Miss Gulch in Kansas—but by defending Toto against the Lion and leading the quest she grows into a responsible moral agent, which is what her delayed homecoming requires.

Altamura and Fritzman argue the film has the tripartite structure of Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit: gray Kansas is a partial truth (thesis), 'somewhere over the rainbow' the antithesis, and the synthesis is Dorothy's discovery that the home she yearned for was Kansas all along—a truth that emerges only through misrecognition, which is why Glinda cannot simply tell her the slippers' power. They read 'Over the Rainbow' through Hegel's 'unhappy consciousness' and side with Hegel's one world against the Kantian two-worlds reading (Kansas as the knowable island, Oz as the unknowable beyond) that they put in the mouths of heckling 'bullies' and detect in Rushdie. Against Rushdie's line that the companions 'already possess what they seek,' they insist the trio really were hollow men who became brainy, tender, and brave through the journey, the Wizard's trinkets supplying Hegelian public recognition. From the Philosophy of History they cast Dorothy as a world-historical individual whose unintentional destruction of both Witches and exposure of the Wizard advances Oz's freedom—Toto's deliberate pulling of the curtain included.

The Bells read Baum's book against Bleeding Kansas and John Brown: 1900 readers, they argue, heard 'Kansas' as the slave-or-free question, making Dorothy the Great Emancipator who frees the Munchkins, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, the Winkies, and finally herself from the Witch's servitude. They pair her with Socrates, recasting the Republic's opening scene at Cephalus's slave-owning mansion (Thrasymachus's 'injustice on a sufficiently large scale' pays) as an abolitionist confrontation, and quoting the Phaedo's claim that philosophy is practicing for death to explain why vastly outnumbered reformers—Socrates, Brown at Harpers Ferry and Osawatomie, Dorothy facing the Witch's forty wolves, forty crows, bee swarms, and Winkie army—do not fear the odds. The shared moral: the love of wisdom, pursued in a community of inquirers, charms away the fear of death, which is why tyrants and slave-owners, whose own best part is enslaved, live in terror and cannot sleep at night.

Curry argues that The Wiz, the all-Black 1978 remake, dramatizes the acquisition of a distinctively Black 'racial virtue'—a habitual excellence defined in quasi-Aristotelian terms and grounded in W.E.B. Du Bois's picture of races as 'vast families' bound by common history and a divinely rooted race feeling (with Alexander Crummell and William H. Ferris as supporting race theorists). Dorothy, a Harlem kindergarten teacher who has never been south of 125th Street, lacks knowledge of self, and each companion personifies a virtue she must claim: the newspaper-stuffed Scarecrow, whose crows' 'crow commandments' and song 'You Can't Win' embody internalized racist miseducation; the Tin Man's capacity for feeling; and Fleetwood Coupe de Ville's courage outside the New York Public Library, glossed through Ferris's call for 'lion-like men.' Evillene's sweatshop creed that 'suffering is food for the soul' personifies the redemptive-suffering myth and failed-integrationism the chapter rejects, while Glinda's 'believe in yourself' and 'A Brand New Day' make honest admittance of racial reality the precondition of 'co-authoring' the world.

book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive
essays: Where Pink Floyd Ends and Radiohead Begins
2. - Radiohead, or the Philosophy of Pop
You’re Living in a Fantasy World, This Beautiful World
Rise and Shine It’s On Again Off Again
Where Tragedy Ends and Community Begins
This Is Really Happening (So Do Something)
Brush the Cobwebs from the Sky, Let the Genie Out from the Bottle
If You Think that You’re Strong Enough . .
A Large Rock Saved My Life
samples: The editors' introduction argues that Radiohead succeeded The Clash as 'the only band that matters' partly for philosophical reasons: rather than stating abstractions, their music points toward analyses of our actual historical situation, showing 'how it should be possible for pop music to incarnate a particular historical situation' (Greif's question). It reads the laser-data 'House of Cards' video as proof that in our world only the underlying data matters, with Radiohead releasing the source code so fans can re-image it themselves. It then previews the volume's encounters: Heidegger's phenomenology and the manipulation of Yorke's voice on Kid A, Marx on the pay-what-you-want release of In Rainbows, and the pathos of Aristotelian tragedy running through the sad songs.

Reisch asks whether Radiohead is the Pink Floyd of the twenty-first century and answers that the comparison misleads: where Barrett-era Floyd used electronics to escape into psychedelic fantasy, Radiohead's apparent space-rock is phenomenological, giving voice to pre-reflective experience of technological modern life. He reads 'No Surprises' (Yorke singing with his head in a filling glass sphere) as a study in the political infantilization of commuters, and OK Computer's car crash ('Airbag'), 'Let Down', and 'Lucky' as registering the feel of a fragile, technology-saturated world. Quoting Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and Chomsky on manufactured consent, he argues we can see no alternative to the technologically rational system, and then, against Descartes' priority of the isolated 'I', invokes Heidegger's Being-in-the-world and Merleau-Ponty's embodied subject to suggest that our deepening immersion in technology may be changing the self itself — the truth the collapsing pedestrians of the 'Just' video cannot face.

Greif asks how pop music could ever 'incarnate a particular historical situation' and answers with Radiohead's portrait of broadcast culture around 2000: an environing, objectless dread in which each person lives at a knot of shouted messages no one sent and complaining only marks you as a crank. The band's turn to electronica was not avant-garde innovation but the discovery of the sound of that second nature, with Yorke's sampled-and-broken voice alternately absorbed into the machine and reasserting the human, and the lyric 'we' sliding between a scared individual lying that he is not alone, a wished-for collectivity, and the ventriloquized tyrant (as with Brecht's Pirate Jenny). Radiohead's church-tinged sublimity observes the storm from inside it — an internalized, inhuman sublime rather than the tradition's safe vantage on crushing power. Pop, he concludes, neither mirrors us nor preaches: it lets us retain and reactivate knowledge social speech forbids, and its deepest effect is not revolution but defiance — the retention of a private voice, a politics of re-created privacy — epitomized by 'There There' warning 'just 'cause you feel it doesn't mean it's there' inside an art form devoted to making you feel.

Sylvia argues that the split-screen 'All I Need' video made for MTV's anti-trafficking EXIT project — an American child's comfortable day intercut with a child laborer finishing the very shoes the American takes off — argues against child labor more powerfully than a standard utilitarian argument, because it joins Aristotle's ethos, pathos, and logos instead of relying on logos alone. Using the cognitive/expressive distinction, he claims the song also argues by turning listeners back on themselves ('I only stick with you because there are no others'). He then deploys Nozick's experience machine: we are all plugged into a Baudrillardian, Matrix-like media hyperreality that can make exploitation fade into background images, and the video's slap in the face 'punctures the hyperreality', showing how emotion can do argumentative work that rigorous argument cannot.

Slowik uses Radiohead's evolution — from the standard pop structures of Pablo Honey and The Bends to the layered, quasi-classical textures of Kid A and Amnesiac ('In Limbo''s independent melodic lines, the wordless climax of 'Pyramid Song') — to introduce the philosophy of music. He weighs what a musical work is, testing nominalism, idealism, and realism against 'Like Spinning Plates' and its live versions, then pits the emotion theory against formalism in explaining how songs like 'Like Spinning Plates' move us. The chapter closes on whether musical experience is universal and on Hume's 'Standard of Taste': if the test of time validates greatness, then the argument over whether OK Computer or In Rainbows is the better album might actually have an objectively right answer.

Surber proposes Kristeva's 'abject aesthetics' as the new pair of shades that makes Radiohead legible: 'Creep' expresses abjection (the creep excluded even from recognition by the beautiful people), the android of 'Paranoid Android' is a borderline phenomenon neither human nor machine, and the bodily imagery of 'Bones', 'My Iron Lung', and the corpse in 'Knives Out' enacts the eruption of the pre-linguistic, formless abject, as do Donwood's dissolving Kid A letters. He contrasts the Beatles' aesthetics of psychedelic transcendence and Pink Floyd's existentialist aesthetics of alienation — built on Sartre's 'Hell is other people' gaze and the being-for-itself/being-in-itself split — with Radiohead's fluid, boundary-less world where meanings never come into focus and no existential revolt is possible because the embodied self is part of the world. Against the charge of nihilism, he reads Hail to the Thief and In Rainbows ('How come I end up where I started?') as postmodern reconstruction: if boundaries and meanings are fluid, they can also be remade.

book: 039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life
essays: That’s His Story and He’s Stickin’ to It
Too Much Tequila, Or Not Quite Enough
Jimmy Buffett “Singer of Inordinate Tunes” and Heideggerian Troubadour
How We Still Might Manage a Smile Being Pirates and Making Meaning
Wonder Why We Ever Go Home
“Where Did All the Good Songs Go ”
samples: The editors argue Buffett is a philosopher despite his own denials, in the sense of Royce and Dewey: philosophy is critical reflection on living that returns to ordinary experience, and Buffett's songs, books, and concerts pass Dewey's test of rendering everyday predicaments 'more significant, more luminous, more fruitful.' They compare 'Margaritaville' to Plato's Republic — not equal in pedigree but equal in kind as occasions for philosophical practice — to defend meaning-making as a democratic practice open to Parrotheads, not just professors. Reading the album 'Changes in Latitudes, Changes in Attitudes' as a guide, they set Buffett's 'Porpoise Driven Life,' where purpose is found by sailing your own waters in the company of friends, against Rick Warren's revelation-based 'Purpose Driven Life.'

Aaron Pratt places Buffett's 'island escapism' in the lineage of the ancient 'graceful life' philosophies: like Diogenes the Cynic, Buffett flouts social convention (pirates over Civil War generals, the beach over the rat race, 'Be good and you will be lonesome'), and like Epicurus he preaches pleasure with prudence rather than mere indulgence. 'Cheeseburger in Paradise' becomes Epicurus's command to know what you want and go get it, while the hung-over confession of 'Margaritaville' — 'I know it's my own damn fault' — supplies the Epicurean proviso that overindulgence ruins the pleasure it promises. The chapter closes by arguing that counter-cultures like Parrotheadism carry built-in safety features: careers and families force Epicurean prudence, keeping escapism a periodic liberation rather than social collapse.

Doug Anderson reads Buffett as an 'American Stoic' — unlike his friend the Cynic Hunter S. Thompson, who dropped out and died, Buffett accepts his fated world of competitive capitalism and controls the one thing Stoics say we can: his own attitudes, 'changes in latitudes, changes in attitudes.' He leans on Seneca's advice to Serenus that wine and dreaming liberate the mind ('drink washes cares away') to interpret the dialectic of dreaming and drinking in 'Margaritaville,' 'Five o'Clock Somewhere,' and 'License to Chill' as Stoic self-renewal — the margarita even frees the singer to admit his own fault — with Emerson's intoxication-speaking poet as the American model. Excess is the failure mode: the expatriates of 'Banana Republics' who mistake the dream for an end state and Buffett's late-thirties hangover reckoning mark the Stoic middle path between deadening routine and 'too much tequila.'

Drew Dalton takes Buffett's claim that 'we don't just enjoy our escapism — we NEED it' as an admission that being itself is burdensome, overturning the Plato–Augustine–Leibniz consensus that it is good to be. Since 'Margaritaville is nowhere' — it is on no map and can never be reached — what we long for is not a better vacation but release from having to be at all, which is why even on holiday in Key West we still dream of escape. Heidegger's Being and Time supplies the framework: thrownness, being-toward-death, anxiety, and guilt reveal existence as a weight we never chose, so the escapist longing to be otherwise than ourselves is the 'inauthentic' flight Heidegger describes (without moral condemnation), and Levinas's On Escape confirms that 'it is precisely from all that is weighty in being that escaping sets forth.'

Phil Oliver pairs Buffett with William James: both hold that philosophy is 'not a technical matter' but each person's sense of what life deeply means, had in non-verbal moments of elevation as much as argued in words. The chapter's core is James's 'moral holiday' — a morally legitimate respite from care and struggle — naturalized in Buffett's 'License to Chill' and 'Trip Around the Sun' ('it's good to know it's out of my control'), joined by James's lightness about error from 'The Will to Believe' and Russell's and Dawkins's responses to cosmic annihilation. Against those who hear mere hedonism, Oliver insists Jamesian holidays are care-free but never care-less: like Thoreau's 'live deliberately' echoed in 'Growing Older But Not Up,' they renew us for the return to work, and James's ambivalence about alcohol in The Varieties of Religious Experience mirrors the risk of Buffett's frozen concoctions.

Amanda Feller reads Buffett's life and lyrics through Jack Mezirow's transformative learning theory: a disorienting dilemma (the Holiday Inn has-been singer, the 1994 seaplane crash, the near-divorce) unhinges one's compass, and growth requires disorientation, framed exploration of one's governing assumptions, and re-orientation. She reads the arc of 'Margaritaville' — 'I know it's nobody's fault' to 'hell, it could be my fault' to 'my own damn fault' — as exactly this movement, and Buffett's post-crash fly-fishing for the small bass as embodied, whole-self reflection through which he 'rediscovered his saline psyche.' The chapter's sharpest warning is that escapism is not transformation: the blogger who moved to the beach found that no matter where you go, there you are, because only introspection, not a change of venue, transforms.

book: 040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind
samples: The editors' introduction frames the volume around First Contact with a robotic civilization: citing SETI's Seth Shostak, they argue aliens are more likely to be AI machines than little green men, with the Autobot-Decepticon civil war catching humans in between on a moral as well as physical plane. They pose the book's questions about Optimus Prime and Megatron: whether Transformers have moral status and minds despite passing the Turing Test, whether they have souls and are capable of Platonic or erotic love, and what makes Optimus the same being whether robot or vehicle. Probing Transformer nature, they conclude, is really probing human nature, since Transformers are our own creations.

Hall predicts what real alien Transformers would be like: any starfaring civilization is at least Kardashev Type 1 and would send nanotechnological, shape-shifting robots rather than biological explorers, since minds upload into machine bodies and colonies go all-robot. He proposes a logarithmic 'Hall scale' of ethics, arguing that interstellar cooperation requires Level 10 morality whose expanding inclusiveness would give visitors enough concern for indigenous species to leave Earth as a nature preserve, since robots need only the matter and energy of Mercury and the outer planets, not our biosphere.

Shook dismantles the four assumptions behind the argument that advanced aliens would already be here (that they want to find us, that travel is easy, that visits would leave traces, and that disguised visitors must be benign), showing the Transformers scenario - a warring robotic civilization that crashes into Earth unnoticed and disguises itself as Chevys and boomboxes like Bumblebee and Frenzy - is more probable than SETI's radio-based angel-alien mythology. War, not peace, drives the technology of real civilizations, as Trailbreaker's 'Simple. Disguise!' explanation of transformation shows, so First Contact will likely be with militaristic strangers absorbed in their own conflicts, not missionaries.

Using the hidden sides of Transformers - a robot inside a Camaro, a tank inside a robot - the authors stage the philosophy of perception: Descartes's innate geometrical rules and Berkeley's bodily cross-referencing both fail to explain how Sam Witwicky can know the steelyard robot is his Camaro, while Merleau-Ponty's embodied account of focus, background, and 'indeterminate vision' explains it through the perceiver's lived body. They extend this to the 'Autobot Spike' mind-transfer episode and to CGI: virtual Transformers on screen feel hollow because light-created images have no hidden surfaces for our bodies to investigate and grasp.

Spicher argues that when Bumblebee trades his beat-up 1976 Camaro for a shiny 2007 model only his appearance changes (an accidental change), never his identity, because transforming is part of a Transformer's essence like a human wearing a mask. Locke's memory continuity and Thomson's bodily criterion each fail - the embryo, coma, and corpse problems, plus the thought experiment of Megatron's memories transplanted into another body - so he defends an Aristotelian composite of form and matter in which the Spark is the soul-like form organizing the machine body, preserving identity through transformation as form guides matter toward actuality.

Steiff reads the 2007 movie as a sustained lesson in perceptual error: Sam's Porsche disappointment at the dealership, the parents' 'earthquake' misperception, and the Camaro that no one at Bobby B's lot suspects show that we see what context, expectation, and conditioning (the kitten experiments) lead us to see. She distinguishes illusion - misperceiving an object really present, as Sam misperceives Bumblebee as just a car - from hallucination, and weighs direct realism against representative realism's 'veil of perception' using film tricks from Melies's jammed camera to the Lumiere brothers' panic-inducing train, leaving Sam's knowledge resting on fallible but indispensable sense experience.

book: 041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)
essays: Where Do We Go from Here
Under-Confidence in Reason Once It’s Easier Said, then It’s Done
Sin, Play, and the “Synagogues of Satan”
But Does Political Satire Promote Democratic Values
Philosophy in the Age of Truthiness
Colbert Is (the Tragedy and Comedy of) America, and So Are We
What Mr. Colbert Has Taught Us (Besides Everything)
Truthiness and the Denial of Responsibility
I’m Done But The Editor Expects Some Sort of Fancy Conclusion
samples: Aaron Allen Schiller's introduction presents Colbert as a cultural institution (Time's 100 Most Influential, Emmy and Peabody awards, a 2008 presidential run) and a faux-pundit who does not report the news but 'feels the news at us' through the WØRD, Better Know a District, the ThreatDown, and the calls to action his fan army, the Colbert Nation, obeys. It argues philosophers love him because he 'tortures logic like Mozart writes symphonies,' playing with Truth and Reality through his coinages truthiness and wikiality so thoroughly that no future philosophical tract on the nature of Truth will be complete without considering truthiness. The book, it says, is for anyone who finds those concepts 'under their skin' without quite knowing why.

David Kyle Johnson argues that Colbert's gut-thinking persona (the Harriet Miers 'I know her heart' bit, 'that's my right' on the Panama Canal) satirizes a real and widespread vice, and he refutes the philosophies behind it. Individual and moral relativism collapse into self-contradiction and absurdity ('Lincoln was not assassinated' would be 'true for' someone; Hitler could not be condemned), while gut-justification is what Locke called 'enthusiasm' - a belief that is 'its own proof,' circular like the prophet whose revelation needs no burning bush. Following Jamie Whyte, he dismantles the 'right to my opinion' (running example: the friend who insists on a grassy-knoll shooter despite the melon-head evidence): there is no epistemic or moral right to undefended belief, and no right to intellectual comfort. Against this he holds up Socrates, wisest because he alone admitted ignorance, and insists philosophy and politics progress only through argument, so truthiness is never an acceptable substitute.

Steven Gimbel reads the Formidable Opponent segment - red-tie Colbert debating blue-tie Colbert - as a glimpse of authentic moral deliberation that the flip-flop-phobic punditry satirized by the show (and Jon Stewart's Crossfire rant) has abandoned. Moral doubt is good because perspectives are partial and the Enlightenment 'marketplace of ideas' of Locke and Mill tests beliefs only through challenge. It has a source: 'morally right' bundles five dimensions - the actor's character shaped by habit (Aristotle's virtue ethics), the act itself judged by Kant's categorical imperative, the pleasure-versus-pain consequences tallied Bentham-style, the rights of the person affected from Locke and Hobbes's social contract, and the special care obligations of close relationships (Noddings and Ruddick) - and hard cases like abortion and flag burning are exactly where these dimensions pull apart. So emulate the dueling Colberts: fear not the flip-flop, since deciding which value trumps which requires open-minded conversation with oneself.

Roben Torosyan turns Colbert into a negative textbook for critical thinking: the character embodies the exact opposite of the American Philosophical Association's seven critical-thinking dispositions (inquisitive, open-minded, truthseeking, systematic, analytical, judicious, confident in reason), from refusing to imagine Lisa Randall's extra dimensions, to 'the market doesn't lie' about the Bible, to placing himself above Maimonides, Socrates, and Aquinas in the stem-cell Formidable Opponent. Each section names the fallacies his shtick commits - appeal to popularity, appeal to ignorance, composition, circular reasoning, wishful thinking, appeal to consequences - using real WØRD bits like the Iraq 'no casualties' monologue and the cake-metaphor exchange about the war. The WØRD's self-undermining bullet points are read as Derridean deconstruction (différance): every assertion shot through with what differs from and defers it. Watching Colbert fail at the examined life Socrates recommended, the viewer learns to catch such abuses in pundits and in themselves.

Rachael Sotos argues the Report performs Platonic play: like the divine puppet of Plato's Laws with its competing cords, Colbert reveals what moves us (fear, hope, the ThreatDown bears, the 'golden cord' of the good) and so teaches freedom through play. Colbert's pompous self-authority - claiming to be 'the canon and measure' of virtue in I Am America - parodies Aristotle's serious man (spoudaios, megalopsychos) and the sophists Protagoras and Prodicus with their Orpheus voices, proving Heraclitus right that 'time is a child at play' and Aristotle wrong that play is mere medicinal rest. Tracking the war on fun from Chrysostom through Aquinas's eutrapelia (there is sin in a lack of play) to Erasmus's Praise of Folly and the Puritans' ban on theaters as 'Synagogues of Satan,' she reads Colbert's playing-at-sin - the man-seed eugenics bit, the 'black friend' boasts, the Ellen DeGeneres Paradox on Wikiality - as Erasmian folly that heals America's Puritan hangover in the culture wars.

Jason Southworth asks how viewers understand Colbert's deliberately confusing coinages ('wordanista,' 'superstantial,' 'Lincolnish,' 'freem,' and the title 'I Am America (And So Can You!)'). Borrowing Russell's view that names abbreviate definite descriptions (the 'spot check test'), he argues these utterances are paraphrasable and therefore meaningful rather than nonsense, distinguishing meaning from reference and literal from non-literal meaning. He then applies Grice's cooperative principle and conversational maxims to derive implicatures: the gut speech violates 'do not say what you believe to be false' and so implies truthiness-as-visceral-feeling, 'wordinista' imports Sandinista-style radicalism, and 'John, tear me a new one' generates the kitten-woodchipper joke. Since context fixes meaning, even dictionary-less words like 'freem' can be decoded, and the Wordinistas at Webster's are unnecessary.

book: 042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward
samples: Editor Ben Dyer's introduction argues that supervillains have effectively 'won' as comics matured: since the 1970s-80s turn (O'Neil/Adams Green Lantern, Miller's Dark Knight Returns, Watchmen), heroes like Batman, Superman, and Spider-Man acquired broken psychologies while villains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Lex Luthor were humanized until hero and villain barely contrast. Citing Stan Lee's claim that the supervillain is the most important character, Dyer announces the volume's project: to restore that contrast by analyzing the villain's relation to morality and society, asking whether tyranny can serve a good cause, whether an all-powerful being is limitless, whether anyone can truly desire evil, and why good henchmen are so hard to find.

Four 'Phase One' essays. Dyer reads Mark Millar's Wanted through Plato's cave: Wesley Gibson escapes a pathetic life like the freed prisoner, but like Adolf Eichmann (via Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem) he murders his conscience, so the Fraternity's consequence-free world leaves him numb and unable to value anything - a descent deeper into the cave, ending in the banality of evil. Novy explains why henchmen betray using Aristotle's utility/pleasure/complete friendship distinction (Big Cheese, Henchmen Muenster and Feta): supervillain gangs are Hobbesian pirate crews with no enforcer, so a modus vivendi of self-interest collapses under interrogation and only Machiavellian fear secures loyalty. Foresman applies Goodman and Rawls's reflective equilibrium as a 'cheat' to rank Apocalypse, Magneto, Luthor, the Joker, and Bizarro, concluding the 'best of the worst' is judged on evil ends (or evil means, as with Magneto) and even on glorious failure. Arinder and Milton, in a staged descent-into-madness frame, diagnose mad science in Victor Frankenstein and Dr. Doom as science that denies value-laden theory choice - impossible because data underdetermine theory - breeding the hubris that dehumanizes the scientist.

Four 'Phase Two' essays on the nature of evil. Arp argues that in V for Vendetta V is a utilitarian user of persons just like the fascist Norsefire state - using Dascombe as a shield and torturing Evey 'for her own good' - so Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means condemns the hero-as-villain, though 'moral autonomy' Kantians complicate the verdict. Poon stages the Aquinas-Ockham debate over will and intellect as Magneto reprograms Sentinels against New York (Ultimate X-Men #05), arguing the will cannot choose against the intellect's judgment, so supervillains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Apocalypse act for what seems good to them with a deeply flawed conception of the good. Robichaud uses Superman Returns, Civil War, and Captain America vs the Red Skull to test Mackie's error theory, prescriptivism, expressivism, and moral relativism, defending moral objectivism against the Modern Age's gray morality. Sylvia IV and Walters use Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures with competent judges, and Railton's ideal-advisor moral realism to dismantle Mojo's defense that his Spineless Ones' ratings-driven bloodsports are just desire-satisfaction, indicting our own reality TV.

Four 'Phase Three' essays on world conquest. Terjesen asks whether Doctor Doom's magnanimity (Aristotle's great-souledness, contra the unity-of-virtues thesis Aquinas held and Philippa Foot qualified) makes him less villainous than The Authority, whose purely consequentialist paternalism - like Doom's Emperor Doom or Ozymandias's plot - usurps a free choice no mere power can justify. Barringer reads Marvel's Civil War through Hobbes: the Stamford explosion and unrestrained superpowers recreate the state of nature, the Registration Act is the surrender of freedom to a sovereign, and Stark, Richards, and Pym repeat Hobbes's flawed faith in 'scientific' deductive politics, sealed by the clone-Thor killing of Goliath. Hillerbrand and Sandburg pit Rorschach's Kantian deontology (no compromise, not even to save the world) against Ozymandias's utilitarian murder of three million New Yorkers in Watchmen, arguing via Laplace's Demon that even Dr. Manhattan - nihilist or Schopenhauerian recluse - cannot verify the outcome, so watchmen can be trusted only by knowing their limits. Ostrander's fictional NSC interview has Amanda Waller's Suicide Squad defended with Benthamite utility, the rejection of natural rights as 'nonsense on stilts,' and the Augustinian just-war criteria of just cause, right intent, and proportionality, while the interviewer exposes how conveniently those limits bend.

Three 'Phase Four' essays. Moseley reads the Joker across Batman #1, The Killing Joke, The Dark Knight, A Death in the Family, and Dark Knight Returns as a 'moral monster' who knowingly does evil - and, following Anscombe and Scanlon's guise-of-the-good analysis, pursues aesthetic 'higher values' in a Camus-like affirmation of the absurd, embracing the irrationality Batman's rational moral order cannot fathom. Levin uses X-gene biology (Beast's explanation in Astonishing X-Men, genotype vs phenotype, M-Day) to strip Magneto's Homo sapiens superior claim of any genetic or phenotypic basis, then argues via the moral community of rational persons (Kant's criterion) that mutants and humans share one moral community, condemning both the Registration Act and mutant separatism. O'Neil's prose piece traces Harvey Dent from Calvinist certainty through the acid that scars him to cosmic doubt - quantum randomness, many worlds, Sartre's condemnation to freedom - until Nietzsche's amor fati lets him embrace duality and let the scarred two-headed coin decide good and evil.

Four 'Phase Five' puzzle essays. Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro use Secret Wars to test omnipotence: the Beyonder, Doom, and Galactus cannot do the logically impossible (no spherical cubes, no stone too heavy to lift), two omnipotent beings collide, and a truly omnipotent being has no desires - so villains can never climb to the top they crave. Matthewson and Wall use Frankfurt cases and reasons-responsive source compatibilism to explain why Eddie Brock is responsible for Venom's villainy (he voluntarily bonded and endorses the symbiote's adjusted psychology) while Anne Weying, horrified by what the symbiote made her do, bears only minimal blame. Pickavance reconstructs the Ship of Theseus with Sandman's 'mansand': combining part exchange with materialism lets Norman Osborn reassemble a duplicate Sandman from his scattered remains, and since neither principle nor soul-dualism comes free, personal identity through material change remains unsolved. Loader argues Brainiac's reinvention as a 'facts and logic' computer embodies disembodied Cartesian AI, so the frame problem (Dennett's exploding robots) and embodied cognition (Clark's Tetris, Dreyfus) suggest his detachment from body and world would make him less, not more, intelligent than the humans he scorns.
